topics.title: Nash and strict Nash equilibria
topics.summary: A Nash strategy pair gives each player a best response; strict Nash requires a strictly best response. In an m×n game, the number of strict equilibria is at most min(m,n), since each opposing strategy permits at most one strict best response. Examples include all outcomes being Nash and a zero-sum game having equilibria.

topics.title: Traveler’s Dilemma and preferences
topics.summary: The materials contrast standard Traveler’s Dilemma reasoning with choices motivated by bounded reasoning or regret. Problem Set 3 asks how equilibria change when both players, or only one, maximize total payoff; its solutions are not supplied.

topics.title: Location and coordination games
topics.summary: Vendor-location prompts consider uniform populations, three vendors, and four discrete apartment locations. A supplied solution says endpoint–middle–endpoint locations are not a Nash equilibrium; for a chopped triangular city, no equilibrium exists because no central point bisects the population in every direction. Coordination prompts include Assurance and meeting games.

topics.title: Sequential and repeated-game reasoning
topics.summary: Backward induction predicts outcomes in sequential Hawk–Dove and finite repeated games. For the supplied infinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, trigger-strategy cooperation requires δ ≥ 1/5; infinite Centipede examples show both always-Pass and always-Keep can be Nash equilibria under the stated payoffs.

topics.title: Hawk–Dove and strategic commitment
topics.summary: The supplied Hawk–Dove game has Nash equilibria (H,D) and (D,H); sequential play with player 1 moving first leads to (H,D) by backward induction. A solution frames the Cuban missile crisis as strategic advantage from announcing a threatening stance first.

topics.title: Payoff transformations and Prisoner’s Dilemma
topics.summary: Multiplying a player’s payoffs by a positive constant or adding a constant preserves that player’s payoff rankings and Nash equilibria. Problem Set 3 asks which x values make a displayed game a Prisoner’s Dilemma or Assurance Game, but provides no answers.

result.overview: Materials cover Nash and strict equilibria, best responses, strategic transformations, location games, sequential and repeated play, and incentive constraints. Some prompts are unsolved questions; the supplied solutions address related but not always identical variants.

topics.title: Nash and strict Nash equilibria
topics.summary: A Nash strategy profile gives each player a best response; strict Nash requires a strictly best response. In an m×n two-player game, strict equilibria number at most min(m,n), since each opponent strategy can support at most one strictly best response. Positive payoff scaling and additive constants preserve best responses.

topics.title: Traveler’s Dilemma and preferences
topics.summary: Changing the objective from individual payoff to total payoff can change best responses and equilibria. Pset 3 asks for equilibria when both players, or only one, is utilitarian; Pset 2 discusses standard analysis and a variant with an added $2 bonus/penalty, where equal bids are Nash and (2,2) is uniquely strict.

topics.title: Coordination, conflict, and sequential moves
topics.summary: Hawk-Dove has asymmetric Nash profiles (H,D) and (D,H); in the supplied sequential version, backward induction yields (H,D). Adding a Moderate action can create (M,M), the only strict equilibrium in the supplied variant. Assurance and Prisoner’s Dilemma illustrate coordination and conflicting incentives.

topics.title: Vendor location games
topics.summary: Location equilibria depend on population geometry and the number of vendors. The materials state that endpoint vendors in a three-vendor line arrangement can profitably move inward, and that a chopped triangular city has no equilibrium; Pset 3 asks about three vendors on a continuous line and two vendors serving four discrete buildings.

topics.title: Repeated games, incentives, and backward induction
topics.summary: For the supplied infinite Prisoner’s Dilemma with trigger strategies, cooperation requires 4/(1−δ) ≥ 5, hence δ ≥ 1/5; finite repetition unravels to defection under common knowledge of rationality. In a later Assurance Game, the maximum punishment is 1, below the 2-point deviation gain, so first-period cooperation cannot be supported.

method: Three fresh production indexer instances. Each cold request is followed by exact same-test cached input on that instance. Provider slot is held across each cold+cached pair; acquisition excluded. The same already-extracted original PDF corpus is used. No question preparation, Jev, microphone or paid voice. Empty application cache does not imply cold provider prompt cache.
comparison: Explicit 32,000-character direct-path override; all original source text, no map stage. Production default unchanged during this experiment. This is an algorithm comparison, not a quote-repair-only timing change.

assessment.limitation: Three samples of one real corpus, not latency percentiles or a guarantee. Source citation coverage is not exhaustive topic coverage; manual guide review is recorded separately.
